Incense is the burning product; myrrh is one of the substances used to make it.
Chrism is holy oil that may contain myrrh, while myrrh is the resin itself.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's church smelled of myrrh during the Christmas Eve service.
examples.professional: The museum's exhibit lists myrrh among the trade goods carried along ancient caravan routes.
examples.analytical: Myrrh carried associations of death and burial, which helps explain why it appears among the gifts of the wise men in Matthew's infancy narrative.

nuance.analogy: Like a bitter herb in a sweet dish, myrrh gives its fragrance a note of sorrow.
nuance.etymology: From Arabic murr, 'bitter', through Greek smyrna and Latin myrrha.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the h, as in 'my-r-h'.
Confusing myrrh with myrtle, which is a different plant.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew mor (מוֹר), 'myrrh'; Greek smyrna (σμύρνα), 'myrrh'. Matthew 2:11 says the magi offered gold, frankincense and myrrh to the child Jesus, presenting myrrh as a costly gift for a king. Mark 15:23 describes wine mixed with myrrh offered to Jesus at the crucifixion, which he refuses. John 19:39 tells how Nicodemus brings a large mixture of myrrh and aloes for Jesus's burial, linking myrrh with death and embalming.

myrrh.etymology: From Middle English *mirre*, from Old English *myrre*, from Latin *myrrha*, from Ancient Greek *μύρρα*,

core.definition: A man's name in the Bible, borne by an Edomite chief descended from Esau and by a Levite ancestor of the prophet Samuel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and finish with a voiceless th, as in 'think'. Do not add an extra vowel before the h.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Nahath is a proper name used in Bible study and religious discussion. Most Americans will only meet it in Scripture, so say it plainly and identify the person by family line.

examples.everyday: My Bible class could not agree who Nahath was, so we checked the genealogies.
examples.professional: In the lesson on Levitical genealogies, I list Nahath among the Kohathite ancestors.
examples.analytical: The genealogy of Nahath in 1 Chronicles 6 places Samuel within the Kohathite line.

common_mistakes: Confusing Nahath with Nahash or Nahor, which are different people.
Stressing the second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Nahath appears as a Kohathite Levite in 1 Chronicles 6:26, in the genealogy that places the prophet Samuel among the Levites. Genesis 36:13 names a Nahath as a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau, a chief among the Edomites. The name's meaning is uncertain.

senses.definition: A trademark, or a distinctive name for a brand, or for a range of products by a single manufacturer.
senses.example: The company that invented the category remains a name brand to this day.

senses.definition: A product having such a mark or name.
senses.example: When it comes to laundry detergent, she always buys a name brand, just to be safe.

core.definition: A product sold under a well-known trademark of a major manufacturer, rather than a store's own or a generic label.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on NAME, with brand weaker. Say the r clearly in brand, as Americans do, and keep the vowel short, as in band. Do not stress BRAND, which is a common mistake.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; implies a known quality, though it can also suggest a higher price.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'name brand' in supermarkets and drugstores to contrast with 'store brand' or 'generic'. 'Brand name' is the more neutral or formal term, used in business and writing. Shoppers may ask 'Is that name brand?' casually. A natural reply is 'No, it's the store brand, and it's just as good.'

distinctions.note: A product sold under a retailer's own label, often cheaper than a name brand.
Usually sold in plain packaging with no brand; typically the lowest-priced option.
Refers to fashion labels with high prices and status, not everyday products.

examples.everyday: I usually get the store brand, but my son insists on name-brand cereal.
examples.professional: We're weighing the name-brand software license against an open-source option, and the support terms are the deciding factor.
examples.analytical: A name brand works as a signal of quality under imperfect information, which is why economists study branding as a source of trust.

nuance.analogy: A name brand is like a signature on a painting: it vouches for the work before you inspect it.
nuance.etymology: Name from Old English nama; brand from Old English brand, meaning torch, later a mark burned on livestock to show ownership.
common_mistakes: Stressing BRAND instead of NAME, which makes the compound sound like an ordinary phrase.
Writing 'name brand cereal' without a hyphen before a noun; American style usually writes name-brand cereal.

senses.definition: To confer with others in order to come to terms or reach an agreement.
To arrange or settle something by mutual agreement.
senses.example: We negotiated the contract to everyone's satisfaction.

senses.definition: To succeed in coping with, getting over or navigating a hazard or obstacle.
senses.example: We negotiated the mountain track with difficulty.

senses.definition: To transfer to another person with all the rights of the original holder; to pass, as a bill.

core.definition: To discuss with others in order to reach an agreement on terms, a price, or a solution.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'GOH.' The 'ti' in the middle sounds like 'sh,' and the final syllable rhymes with 'eight.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting a cooperative process.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use negotiate in work, business, and personal situations, such as negotiating a salary or a contract. In casual talk, people often say 'work out a deal' or 'figure something out.' You can also negotiate with a person, or negotiate a deal, a price, or an obstacle.

distinctions.note: Bargain is more informal and focuses on haggling over price, while negotiate covers a wider range of terms and conditions.
Discuss means to talk about something, while negotiate means to talk with the aim of reaching a binding agreement.

examples.everyday: I tried to negotiate a lower rent with my landlord, but he would not budge.
examples.professional: We need to negotiate a timeline with the vendor before the contract is signed.
examples.analytical: A fair theory of justice must explain how rational people can negotiate principles they will live under.

nuance.analogy: To negotiate is like two people carrying a couch through a doorway, adjusting their grip until both can get through.
nuance.etymology: From Latin negotiatus, past participle of negotiari, 'to carry on business,' from negotium.
common_mistakes: Using 'negotiate about' in the wrong place; Americans usually say 'negotiate with someone' or 'negotiate terms.'
Pronouncing the middle 'ti' as 't' rather than 'sh.'

senses.definition: Effeminacy; indulgence in soft living or luxuriousness.
senses.example: Her father warned that luxury and niceness would make the young prince weak.

senses.definition: Fastidiousness; fine sensitivity.
senses.example: Her niceness about table manners drove the cooks wild, since every fork had to be perfect.

senses.definition: Pleasantness, especially of behavior or personality; agreeableness.
A value determining how much processor time to concede to a running process. (See also nice (verb), renice.)
senses.example: Set a higher niceness for the backup job so it yields CPU time to interactive programs.

core.definition: The quality of being pleasant, kind, and agreeable, especially in a person's behavior or personality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -ness is short and unstressed, with a quick i like the vowel in bit, not a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Positive in everyday speech, though it can sound faint or bland when used alone; people often say niceness when they mean warmth that lacks real substance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use niceness to describe a pleasant personality, as in She has a lot of niceness. It is informal and softer than kindness. Americans often add a qualifier, such as underneath all the niceness, to suggest a hidden toughness or to imply that someone is too agreeable.

distinctions.note: Kindness implies active care for others; niceness is a more surface pleasantness that may not involve real help or sacrifice.
Politeness is observing good manners; niceness is a broader warmth of manner and attitude.
Friendliness describes openness toward others; niceness can also cover pleasant but emotionally distant behavior.

examples.everyday: Her niceness is the first thing I notice about her, even on a bad day.
examples.professional: In performance reviews, the manager valued niceness less than the ability to deliver results.
examples.analytical: The novel treats niceness as a social performance, showing how its gentleness can conceal indifference.

nuance.analogy: Like a warm room with the heat turned low: pleasant to be in, but it may not be the kind of warmth that gets things done.
nuance.etymology: Nice (from Latin nescius, meaning ignorant) plus the suffix -ness, forming an abstract noun.
common_mistakes: Confusing niceness with nicety, which means a fine detail or precise distinction.
Using niceness in serious moral contexts where kindness or compassion is the better word.

senses.definition: The time when the Sun is below the horizon when the sky is dark.
senses.example: Most animals are awake at day and sleep at night.

senses.definition: A period of time often defined in the legal system as beginning 30 minutes after sunset, and ending 30 minutes before sunrise.
senses.example: The statute made the break-in a felony because it happened at night.

senses.definition: An evening or night spent at a particular activity.
senses.example: a night on the town

senses.definition: A day, or at least a night.
senses.example: I stayed my friend's house for three nights.

senses.definition: Nightfall.
senses.example: from noon till night

senses.definition: Darkness (due to it being nighttime).
senses.example: The cat disappeared into the night.

senses.definition: A dark blue color, midnight blue.
senses.example: night:

senses.definition: The period of darkness beginning at the end of evening astronomical twilight when the sun is 18 degrees below the horizon, and ending at the beginning of morning astronomical twilight.
senses.example: The telescope recorded faint galaxies only during the night, when the sun was well below the horizon.

senses.definition: A night's worth of competitions, generally one game.
senses.example: The Yankees lost the first night of the four-game series in the rain.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of good night.
senses.example: Night, y'all! Thanks for a great evening!

senses.definition: To spend a night (in a place), to overnight.
senses.example: The hikers decided to night at the lodge rather than push on to the summit.

core.definition: The period of darkness between sunset and sunrise, when the sky is dark and most people sleep.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long i and a clear final t. Do not add a vowel after the t, and do not flap the t, since it is a stop before a pause.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can suggest rest, romance, or danger depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say tonight for this evening, and last night for yesterday evening. Good night is said when leaving or going to bed, not as an arrival greeting, where good evening is more natural. Americans say at night for a general time and in the night for a specific event or period.

distinctions.note: Evening runs roughly from sunset until bedtime, while night usually means the later, darker hours.
Overnight describes something happening during the night or lasting from one day to the next, such as an overnight flight.

examples.everyday: We stayed up late talking last night, so I'm exhausted this morning.
examples.professional: We're on the night shift this week, so please send me the report before six.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers have used night as a metaphor for uncertainty that reason struggles to illuminate.

nuance.analogy: Night is the shadow half of the day, the stretch when the sun leaves the sky to the stars and streetlights.
nuance.etymology: From Old English niht, from Proto-Germanic *nahts.
common_mistakes: Saying good night as a greeting when you arrive somewhere; use good evening instead.
Using in the night for general times; at night is more common for regular or general periods.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word laylah means night, the period of darkness. Genesis 1:5 names the darkness Night in the account of creation. Psalm 30:5 says weeping may last for the night, but joy comes in the morning. First Thessalonians 5:2 says the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.

night.etymology: From Middle English *nighte,night,nyght,niȝt,naht*, from Old English *niht*, from **naht* (“night”), from Proto-Germanic **nahts* (“night”), from Proto-Indo-European **nókʷts* (“night”).

senses.definition: The quality or state of being noble; nobility or grandeur.
senses.example: Her quiet nobleness during the crisis impressed everyone who witnessed how she treated others.

core.definition: The quality of being morally admirable, generous, and honorable in character.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is quick and reduced, so say it as 'NOH-buhl-nuhs,' not 'NOH-bluh-ness.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises moral character and generosity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'nobleness' rarely, and it sounds old-fashioned or literary. In everyday speech they say 'nobility' or 'nobleness of character' in formal writing, and 'goodness' or 'integrity' in casual talk.

distinctions.note: 'Nobility' is the more common form in modern American English and can also mean a social class, while 'nobleness' refers mainly to moral quality.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's nobleness of heart is something everyone in the family admires.
examples.professional: In the performance review, the manager praised her nobleness of purpose in helping new hires.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that nobleness of character cannot be reduced to social rank, since it depends on the will to act justly.

nuance.analogy: Like a cathedral's quiet dignity: it does not shout, but it stands tall and admirable.
nuance.etymology: From 'noble' (Latin nobilis) plus the suffix '-ness,' meaning the state or quality of being noble.
common_mistakes: Using 'nobleness' in everyday speech where 'nobility' or 'goodness' sounds more natural.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full 'ble' instead of a reduced vowel.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to non-Euclidean geometry.

core.definition: Relating to geometries that reject or modify Euclid's parallel postulate, such as hyperbolic or elliptic geometry.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on KLID, in the middle of the word, and non carries secondary stress. Euclid starts with yoo, and the -ean ending is pronounced ee-un.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise mathematical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adjective in mathematics, physics and philosophy of science, usually with the noun geometry, as in non-Euclidean geometry. It rarely appears alone in casual talk. In print it is hyphenated, and Euclidean is always capitalized.

distinctions.note: Euclidean describes the familiar geometry of flat planes with parallel lines; non-Euclidean describes systems where the parallel postulate fails.
Hyperbolic geometry is one non-Euclidean geometry; non-Euclidean covers the whole family.

examples.everyday: I read about non-Euclidean geometry last night and started wondering whether my kitchen floor is really flat.
examples.professional: The navigation model assumes a non-Euclidean space, because distances on a sphere do not follow straight Euclidean lines.
examples.analytical: Riemann's work showed that a consistent non-Euclidean geometry could be built by altering assumptions about parallel lines.

nuance.analogy: Like measuring a city map drawn on a curved globe, where two straight paths can meet at the poles.
nuance.etymology: Named after Euclid (Greek Eukleidēs, around 300 BCE), the mathematician who systematized geometry.
common_mistakes: Spelling it Euclidian; the standard spelling is Euclidean.
Treating non-Euclidean as a single geometry; it names a whole family of geometries.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being nonintentional.

core.definition: The quality of not being intended or done on purpose; in philosophy, lacking intentional content or aboutness.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on NAL, in the -ality ending, not on TEN. The -tion is pronounced shun, and the early syllables non-in are light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a quality without judging the person, though in legal or moral discussion it can be used to excuse harm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this noun mainly in philosophy of mind, law and psychology. In everyday speech people say unintentional or accidental, which sound natural in conversation. Use nonintentionality when you want to talk about the quality itself, not a single act.

distinctions.note: Unintentionality is the everyday word for the quality of not meaning to do something; nonintentionality is more abstract and technical.
In philosophy, intentionality means aboutness, the directedness of a mental state toward an object; nonintentionality is its absence, not a moral lack of purpose.

examples.everyday: He kept stressing the nonintentionality of the mistake, so I knew he felt terrible about it.
examples.professional: In the incident review, we treated the nonintentionality of the failure as a root-cause question, not a question of blame.
examples.analytical: Brentano made intentionality the mark of the mental, which makes the nonintentionality of physical processes philosophically significant.

nuance.analogy: Like a leaf blown across a yard: it moves and changes things, but nothing in it is aiming at a destination.
nuance.etymology: Built from non- plus intentionality, from Latin intendere, 'to stretch toward, aim at'.
common_mistakes: Confusing nonintentionality with intentionality, which in philosophy means aboutness rather than purpose.
Using the noun in casual speech where unintentional or accidental is more natural.

senses.definition: Not living; inanimate.
senses.example: Biologists distinguish living cells from nonliving matter like rock, water, and dust.

core.definition: Not alive; lacking the characteristics of life such as growth, metabolism and reproduction.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIV, the root, not on the prefix non-. The -ing is a short ihng, not eeng, so say LIV-ing with a short i in the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain descriptive term, used in science, education and everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nonliving in science classes, environmental discussions and general conversation about things like rocks, water and air. It refers to things that were never alive, so for organisms that have died people usually say dead. In casual speech people often say things like rocks or water instead.

distinctions.note: Dead describes an organism that was once alive; nonliving describes things that have never been alive, such as rocks or water.
Inanimate is broader and can describe objects or an unlively mood; nonliving is the standard scientific term for things without life.

examples.everyday: The kids were learning that rocks and water are nonliving, while plants and animals are living.
examples.professional: Our data pipeline removes nonliving entries, such as device placeholders, before the analysis starts.
examples.analytical: Aristotle distinguished living from nonliving bodies by the presence of a soul, or principle of life.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone in a garden: it stays in the same place while a plant grows around it.
nuance.etymology: From non- plus living, from Old English libban, 'to live'.
common_mistakes: Using nonliving to mean dead; for organisms that have died, American speakers usually say dead.
Confusing living with lively, which is an adjective of energy rather than a biological state.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew chay means living, and nephesh chayyah means living creature or living being. Genesis 1:20 (RSV) describes living creatures filling the waters, and Genesis 2:7 (RSV) says the man became a living being. Psalm 115:4-7 (RSV) describes idols as lifeless, with mouths that do not speak, which shows the Hebrew Scriptures contrasting living God with nonliving objects of worship.

senses.definition: Not any thing; no thing.
senses.example: Don't just say nothing. Tell me what's going on.

senses.definition: An absence of anything, including empty space, brightness, darkness, matter, or a vacuum.
senses.example: Out past the last star there was nothing but cold, silent darkness.

senses.definition: Something trifling, or of no consequence or importance.
senses.example: - What happened to your face?- It's nothing.

senses.definition: A trivial remark especially in the term sweet nothings.
senses.example: Don't worry about her, she only whispers sweet nothings to everyone at parties.

senses.definition: A nobody (insignificant person).
senses.example: Back in high school, he was a nothing, but now he runs the company.

senses.definition: Used to dismiss a previous statement.
senses.example: - Wait a moment.- Wait nothing! I'm going after them.

senses.definition: Completely unimportant.
senses.example: Dallas scored on what had seemed until then like a nothing play.

senses.definition: Lacking effort or commitment.
senses.example: The cricketer played a nothing shot.

senses.definition: Never mind; it's not important; forget what I said.
senses.example: Nothing, never mind; forget I asked about the report, it's not important.

core.definition: Not anything at all; no thing or amount of something.

pronunciation.tip: Start the word with a voiceless th, with the tongue between the teeth, and avoid turning it into an f, t, or d sound. In fast speech the ending sounds like 'nuh-thin.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be cheerful in replies like 'Nothing much,' but negative when it means something has no value.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nothing constantly in casual conversation, especially in answers like 'Nothing much' to 'What's up?' It also appears in phrases like 'It's nothing' as a polite reply to thanks. In formal writing, 'nothing' is used in its basic sense, and double negatives such as 'I don't have nothing' are considered nonstandard.

distinctions.note: None refers to a set of people or things that could be counted, while nothing refers to no thing or no matter.
Nobody refers to a person, while nothing refers to things or abstract matters.
No is a determiner placed before a noun, while nothing stands alone as a pronoun.

examples.everyday: Nothing much happened at work today, just the usual emails and a long meeting.
examples.professional: There's nothing in the data that contradicts our hypothesis, so we can move forward with the test.
examples.analytical: Parmenides argued that nothing cannot be thought or spoken, so it cannot be an object of knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Nothing is like an empty room: the walls are there, but no furniture or people fill it.
nuance.etymology: Old English nan thing, 'not any thing.'
common_mistakes: Using a double negative such as 'I don't have nothing'; say 'I don't have anything.'
Pronouncing the th as an f, t, or d sound, so the word sounds like 'nuffing' or 'noting.'
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, the Greek ouden (nothing, or not at all) expresses how human achievement without love counts for nothing before God. First Corinthians 13:2 says that even great faith and knowledge, without love, make a person nothing. Galatians 6:3 warns that someone who thinks himself something when he is nothing deceives himself.

nothing.etymology: From Middle English *nothyng*, *noon thing*, *non thing*, *na þing*, *nan thing*, *nan þing*, from Old English *nāþing*, *nān þing* (“nothing”), equivalent to *no* + *thing*.

senses.definition: Newly made, formed or evolved; having no precedent; of recent origin; new.
senses.example: Researchers developed a novel method for detecting fraud in streaming data.

senses.definition: Original, especially in an interesting way; new and striking; not of the typical or ordinary type.
senses.example: Her approach to teaching was novel, mixing poetry with spreadsheets to explain statistics.

senses.definition: A work of prose fiction, longer than a novella.
senses.example: She spent the weekend reading a novel about a family farm during the Depression.

senses.definition: (historical) A fable; a short tale, especially one of many making up a larger work.
senses.example: The collection contains a novel about a clever fox who outwits the village priest.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A new legal constitution.
senses.example: The reformers drafted a novel constitution that replaced the old royal charter.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: New and different from anything that existed before; original in a way that is interesting or unusual.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'NAH-vul'. Do not say 'NO-vell' with a long o and a clear 'ell'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most uses, implying creativity and originality; it can sound hyped in marketing if overused.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'novel' in professional, academic, and scientific writing to describe a new method or idea that did not exist before, as in 'a novel approach'. In casual speech, 'new' or 'different' is more common. 'Novel' as a noun means a long work of fiction, and the adjective and noun are pronounced the same way.

distinctions.note: 'New' only says something has appeared recently, while 'novel' says it is original in kind and not just a recent version.
'Original' emphasizes that something comes first, while 'novel' emphasizes that it is different from what is typical.
'Unprecedented' is stronger and means there is no earlier example, while 'novel' is a more measured word for something new in approach.

examples.everyday: My sister came up with a novel way to organize our closet, using baskets for every season.
examples.professional: The team proposed a novel method for detecting data drift that does not require labeled examples.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard's account of faith is novel in that it places the individual's choice at the center of religious truth.

nuance.analogy: A recipe no one has cooked before, rather than a new version of a familiar dish.
nuance.etymology: From Latin novellus, 'new', a diminutive of novus, 'new'.
common_mistakes: Using 'novel' in casual speech where 'new' or 'different' sounds more natural.
Pronouncing it as 'NO-vell' with a long o and a clear final 'ell'.

novel.etymology: From Middle English *novel*, from Old French *novel* (“new, fresh, recent, recently made or done, strange, rare”) (modern *nouvel*, *nouveau*), from Latin *novellus* (“new, fresh, young, modern”), diminutive of *novus* (“new”).

senses.definition: Having a nucleus; nucleated.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the nucleate cells stood out clearly after the dye was applied.

senses.definition: To form (into) a nucleus, or to act as a nucleus.
Any salt of a nucleic acid.
senses.example: The chemist dissolved the sodium nucleate in buffer before running the assay.

core.definition: To form a center around which something gathers, such as crystals, bubbles or droplets, or to serve as that center.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, NOO. The verb ends in a clear 'ayt', while the adjective is often said 'NOO-klee-it'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term rather than an emotional word.
nuance.usage_note: Nucleate is used mainly in physics, chemistry, meteorology and materials science, such as water droplets nucleating around dust. Americans rarely use it in casual speech. In everyday talk they would say form, start or gather around.

distinctions.note: Crystallize is a general word for forming crystals; nucleate names the first step, where a seed center forms.
Initiate means to start anything; nucleate specifically means forming a center around which a structure or process grows.

examples.everyday: The forecaster said the storm will probably nucleate over the lake this afternoon.
examples.professional: A small volunteer team nucleated around two engineers who wanted to rebuild the dashboard.
examples.analytical: Dust and sea-salt particles often nucleate water droplets, which is why clouds need aerosols to produce rain.

nuance.analogy: Like a pearl forming around a grain of sand, the material gathers around one tiny first seed.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nucleus, 'kernel', with the verb ending -ate.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as in noo-klee-AYT; the stress belongs on NOO.
Treating the noun nucleate, meaning a salt of a nucleic acid, as a common word; it is specialized chemistry.

senses.definition: A pointer that does not point to any data object.

core.definition: In programming, a pointer value that deliberately refers to no object or memory location, used to signal that there is nothing to point to.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on POINT, the first syllable of pointer, with a light secondary stress on NUL. The final -er is a reduced American r-colored vowel, so do not say 'pointer' with a full 'ah' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a neutral technical term, but a null pointer dereference is usually discussed as a bug.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers in the US use this term daily in C, C++, Java and Rust discussions, often in the phrase 'null pointer exception' (Java) or 'segfault from a null pointer.' In casual conversation, people may just say 'a null pointer bug.' It is not used outside technical contexts.

distinctions.note: A null pointer points to nothing on purpose, while a dangling pointer still holds an address that refers to memory that has already been freed.
A null pointer is a reference to no object, while a null value in a database means missing or unknown data.

examples.everyday: Sorry, the app crashed again, something about a null pointer, the developer says.
examples.professional: The crash report shows a null pointer dereference in the image loader, so we need a guard before that line.
examples.analytical: A null pointer makes absence explicit in the type system, but it also invites errors when programmers forget the check.

nuance.analogy: Like a street sign that points to an empty lot: the sign exists, but following it leads nowhere.
nuance.etymology: 'Null' comes from Latin nullus, 'not any'; 'pointer' comes from 'point' with the agent suffix '-er'.
common_mistakes: Treating 'null pointer' as the number zero; it is a special reference value, not an integer.
Forgetting the second word in spoken English: say NUL POYN-ter, with the stress on POINT.

senses.definition: Someone who is crazy (insane).
senses.example: Some nut job from the government actually thought he could tax our moonshine!

core.definition: Informal slang for someone who is crazy, erratic or behaves in a wild, unpredictable way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, NUT, with a lighter secondary stress on 'job'. The vowel in 'job' is the short 'ah' of 'Bob' in General American, not an 'oh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative and insulting; it is harsh, and it can be used playfully among friends but should be avoided with people who have mental illness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nutjob casually to describe a rude, erratic or extreme person ('some nutjob cut me off'). It is an insult, so it can offend or hurt people, and it should not be used at work or in serious discussions about mental health. A natural reply is 'Yeah, he is a total nutjob' or 'Ha, do not engage with him.'

distinctions.note: Nut is shorter and even more casual; nutjob is a slightly stronger, more insulting way of saying someone is crazy.
Crackpot describes someone with strange, unfounded ideas; nutjob suggests erratic or unstable behavior more generally.
Lunatic is more literal and sometimes old-fashioned; nutjob is a casual slang insult.

examples.everyday: Some nutjob cut me off on the freeway and then started honking like crazy.
examples.professional: Let us not let one nutjob in the comments derail the launch, since our support team can handle him.
examples.analytical: Labels such as nutjob reduce complex mental struggles to a single insult, which discourages honest conversation about illness.

nuance.analogy: A nutjob is like a loose screw in the machine: unpredictable and hard to fix.
nuance.etymology: Blend of nut, slang for a crazy person, and job, whose origin in this sense is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using nutjob in formal writing or professional settings, where it sounds rude.
Pronouncing the vowel in job as 'oh' (JOHB) instead of the short 'ah' of General American.

senses.definition: An evergreen tree (Myristica fragrans) cultivated in the East Indies for its spicy seeds.
senses.example: The botanist photographed a nutmeg tree growing near the volcanic slopes of Grenada.

senses.definition: The aromatic seed of this tree, used as a spice.
The powdered seed, ready for use.
senses.example: Add a pinch of nutmeg to the white sauce just before it thickens.

senses.definition: A whole nutmeg seed.
senses.example: She grated a whole nutmeg over the eggnog, which tasted far better than the powder.

senses.definition: A small moth, Hadula trifolii, feeding on plants and native to the Northern Hemisphere.
senses.example: The entomologist trapped a nutmeg in the clover field, noting its mottled wings.

senses.definition: A gray-brown color.
senses.example: She painted the nursery walls in a soft nutmeg that looked warm in the afternoon light.

senses.definition: The playing of the ball between the legs of an opponent.
senses.example: The crowd roared when he scored after a nutmeg through the defender's legs.

senses.definition: To flavor with nutmeg.
senses.example: She decided the eggnog was lacking in flavor, so she decided to nutmeg it heavily.

senses.definition: To play the ball between the legs of (an opponent).
senses.example: The winger nutmegged the defender twice before crossing the ball to the striker.

core.definition: A brown spice made by grinding the seed of a tropical evergreen tree, used in baking, eggnog, and sweet dishes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, 'NUT.' The second syllable rhymes with 'egg,' so don't say 'nut-MEG' or 'nut-MAYG.' The final g is a hard 'g' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive and warm. It suggests holiday baking, comfort food, and home cooking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nutmeg mainly in baking, especially pumpkin pie, apple pie, and eggnog around the winter holidays. It is sold ground in small jars near the cinnamon in grocery stores, and many cooks grate whole nutmeg with a microplane for better flavor. In sports, 'to nutmeg' is an informal verb in soccer, meaning to pass the ball between an opponent's legs, and Americans who follow soccer use it that way.

distinctions.note: Mace is the lacy red covering of the same seed, with a milder, slightly different flavor, and it is used in similar dishes.
Cinnamon comes from tree bark and is sweeter and more woody, while nutmeg is warmer and more nutty.

examples.everyday: Can you add a pinch of nutmeg to the sweet potatoes before we put them in the oven?
examples.professional: The bakery's new pumpkin latte recipe uses a light dusting of nutmeg, so please update the ingredient list.
examples.analytical: Nutmeg's history in the spice trade shows how a small seed shaped European economic and colonial ambitions.

nuance.analogy: Nutmeg is like the warm, familiar scent of a holiday kitchen, something you notice before you see anything else.
nuance.etymology: From Old French nois muguete, 'musky nut,' with the name later altered in English.
common_mistakes: Saying 'nut-MEG' with the stress on the second syllable.
Using too much nutmeg, which can taste bitter or cause harm if eaten in large amounts.

nutmeg.etymology: From Middle English *notemege*, *notemuge*, a partial translation of Medieval Latin *nux muga*, a variant of Medieval Latin *nux muscata* (“musky nut”).

senses.definition: (obsolete) Wandering about; a casual outing.
senses.label: obsolete

core.definition: A walk or wandering about, especially a casual outing. This sense is obsolete, so Americans would not use it today.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -LAY-. The middle syllables are reduced, so 'bam-byuh' sounds quick and light, not like 'bam-bew-lay-shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds whimsical and old-fashioned, which can be charming in writing or a deliberate joke.
nuance.usage_note: This word is obsolete and does not appear in ordinary American speech. You would not use it in modern conversation without sounding like you were joking or quoting an old book. For a natural alternative, say 'a walk,' 'a stroll,' or 'a quick trip around the block.' Its close relative ambulation, meaning walking, is still used in medicine and physical therapy.

distinctions.note: Stroll is the everyday American word for a relaxed walk. Obambulation is archaic and mostly found in older literature.
Ambulation is still used in medicine for the ability to walk. Obambulation is an obsolete word for wandering about.

examples.professional: The consultant's report called the site visit an obambulation rather than a formal inspection, which was a bit too cute for a client memo.
examples.analytical: Victorian novels often use the leisurely obambulation as a device for introducing a landscape and the social world of a village.

nuance.analogy: Like a vintage coat in a modern closet: it still works, but people stop and look at it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obambulare, to walk about, from ob- (about) and ambulare (to walk).
common_mistakes: Using the word in modern conversation, where it sounds odd or archaic. Say 'stroll' or 'walk' instead.
Stressing the first syllable, as in OB-am-bu-lation, instead of the -LAY- syllable.

senses.definition: Something that is obscene.
senses.example: Martha wouldn't go into the art museum because, as she put it, "They have obscenities just sitting out, on display!"

senses.definition: An act of obscene behavior.
senses.example: Bestiality was outlawed as an obscenity in the strongly conservative community.

senses.definition: Specifically, an offensive word; a profanity; a dirty word.
senses.example: Eliza couldn't stand her daughter's music; as she saw it, it was just shouted obscenities and a heavy drum beat.

senses.definition: Lewdness, indecency, or offensive behavior or material.
senses.example: The coalition of religious conservatives was campaigning against, in their view, rampant obscenity in the entertainment industry.

senses.definition: The fact of being obscene.
senses.example: The committee debated the obscenity of the lyrics before deciding whether the album could be sold.

core.definition: Something that is shockingly offensive, especially sexual material or a rude word that breaks social taboos.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEN, and the final -ity is a weak ih-tee sound. Americans often reduce the middle vowel strongly, so say it quickly.

nuance.connotation: Negative, implying something shameful, offensive or morally wrong.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, obscenity often means a swear word, especially in phrases like shouting obscenities or a string of obscenities. In legal and media contexts it refers to sexual material judged to violate community standards. Be careful: calling someone's language obscene can sound judgmental.

distinctions.note: Profanity is disrespectful or blasphemous language; obscenity can mean profane words but also sexual or indecent material.
Swear word is a casual everyday term for a rude word; obscenity is more formal and can be broader.
Vulgarity is crude behavior or language in general; obscenity is more intense and often legal or moral in tone.

examples.everyday: He yelled a string of obscenities when the car cut him off in traffic.
examples.professional: The content moderation policy removes posts with explicit obscenity, but borderline cases go to human review.
examples.analytical: The court struggled to define obscenity in a way that protected expression while still addressing material that harms minors.

nuance.analogy: An obscenity is like a crack in a clean window: it breaks the expected surface and draws everyone's eye.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obscaenus, ill-omened or indecent.
common_mistakes: Using obscenity to mean only sexual content; in everyday speech it often means swear words.
Confusing obscene with obscure, which means hard to understand.

senses.definition: A structure used to view events from a long distance and to create a full 360 degree range of vision.
senses.example: The ranger climbed the observation tower to scan the valley for wildfire smoke in every direction.

core.definition: A tall, free-standing structure with an elevated platform where people can look out over a wide area.

pronunciation.tip: Stress VAY in observation and TOW in tower, and let the first word be weaker. Tower ends in an r-colored schwa, so don't say 'toe-er'. The 'ow' is the diphthong in 'how'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a scenic view, a place to relax or a sightseeing stop.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase for a free-standing lookout, often at a park, zoo, airport or state site. A building's top floor is more often called an observation deck. A natural reply to the suggestion is 'Sounds good, let's go up before dinner.'

distinctions.note: An observation deck is an open viewing area on a building; an observation tower stands alone and is taller.
A lookout is any spot for watching, while observation tower names a built structure for visitors.
A watchtower is built for guarding or warning; an observation tower is built for viewing scenery or events.

collocations: observation tower at the state park

examples.everyday: Let's go up the observation tower before we leave the park.
examples.professional: Facilities wants to reopen the observation tower for the conference visitors next month.
examples.analytical: The observation tower makes the city legible from above, turning a sprawl of streets into a readable plan.

nuance.analogy: Like a lighthouse for land: it stands high so you can see far in every direction.
nuance.etymology: Observation from Latin observare 'to watch over'; tower from Latin turris.
common_mistakes: Calling it an observatory, which is a building for astronomy.
Stressing the wrong part of observation; the main stress is on VAY, not ob.

senses.definition: A clay earth pigment containing silica, aluminum and ferric oxide.
senses.example: The cave painters mixed red ochre with animal fat to create the bison on the wall.

senses.definition: A somewhat dark yellowish orange color.
senses.example: ochre:

senses.definition: Any of various brown-colored hesperiid butterflies of the genus Trapezites.
senses.example: Along the trail we spotted a small ochre butterfly resting on the grass.

senses.definition: The stop codon sequence "UAA".
senses.example: The sequence ends at the ochre codon UAA, which signals the ribosome to stop translation.

senses.definition: (dated) Money, especially gold.
senses.example: In the old novel, the outlaw hid his ochre under the floorboards before the sheriff arrived.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Having a yellow-orange color.
senses.example: She painted the nursery walls a warm ochre, like sunlight through amber glass.

senses.definition: Referring to cultures that covered their dead with ochre.
senses.example: The excavation revealed an ochre burial in which the dead had been dusted with red pigment.

senses.definition: To cover or tint with ochre.
senses.example: Before the ceremony, the elders ochred their bodies with powdered clay for protection.

core.definition: A yellowish-brown or yellow-orange earth pigment, or the muted yellow-orange color it produces.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -re is pronounced like -er. Do not pronounce the r as a separate sound or add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a color or material; it can be used positively in art or design talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually spell the word ocher, and ochre is the British-style spelling, though both are understood in art and design. You will mostly hear it in painting, archaeology or interior design. In everyday talk, people more often say yellow-brown or golden brown.

distinctions.note: Umber is a darker brown earth pigment, while ochre is yellower and lighter.
Mustard is a bright yellow with a greenish tint, while ochre is a warmer, duller yellow-orange.

examples.everyday: The walls in the new café are a warm ochre, which makes the place feel cozy.
examples.professional: The design team chose an ochre accent color for the website banner to match the brand's earthy palette.
examples.analytical: Ochre pigment has been used since prehistory, and its chemical composition of iron oxides explains its stable yellow-orange color.

nuance.analogy: Ochre is like the color of old parchment or dry autumn leaves.
nuance.etymology: From French ocre, from Greek ōchros, meaning pale yellow.
common_mistakes: Writing ochre when an American text would normally use ocher.
Pronouncing the final -re as a separate syllable.

ochre.etymology: From Old French *ocre* and its source Latin *ōchra*, from Ancient Greek *ὤχρα* (“pale yellow”), from *ὠχρός* (“pale, ocher”).

senses.definition: Synonym of off the rip.
senses.example: She jumped into the argument off rip, without hearing either side.

core.definition: Immediately, from the very beginning, without any delay, warm-up, or preparation.

pronunciation.tip: RIP gets the main stress and has a short i vowel. The r is strongly American, so keep it clearly pronounced and don't let 'off' blend into 'of'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly positive, suggesting speed and directness.
nuance.usage_note: This is an informal and less widespread variant of 'off the rip', heard mainly in some regions, especially the American South, and in relaxed speech. Americans often choose 'right away', 'from the start', or 'right off the bat' in professional settings. Avoid it in writing unless you are quoting speech.

distinctions.note: Both mean immediately, but 'off the rip' is the fuller and more widely used form.
'Off the bat' is more common across the US and is standard in sports and business talk, while 'off rip' is informal and regional.

examples.everyday: She told me off rip that the dinner plan was a bad idea.
examples.professional: The vendor gave us the price off rip, which saved a week of back and forth.
examples.analytical: The essay's opening paragraph states its thesis off rip, a casual tone that suits the argument's confidence.

nuance.analogy: Like a race car leaving the starting line at full throttle.
common_mistakes: Using it in formal writing; 'from the outset' or 'immediately' is better there.
Assuming it is the standard form; many American speakers would say 'off the rip' or 'right off the bat' instead.

core.definition: A woman in the Bible, one of Esau's wives, and the name of a clan chief among his descendants (Edom).

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the fourth syllable, 'BAH', which uses the American open 'ah' vowel. The final syllable is a reduced schwa, so say it lightly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical name in a genealogy and carries no strong judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans would use this name in Bible study or academic discussions of Genesis and Edom. The Revised Standard Version spells it 'Aholibamah'; both forms are seen in study materials. It is a proper name, so it is capitalized.

distinctions.note: Oholibamah is a personal and clan name in Genesis; Oholibah is a symbolic name for Jerusalem in Ezekiel. They are unrelated.

examples.everyday: At our church study we talked about Esau's wife, Oholibamah, and how her family line is part of Genesis.
examples.professional: In the genealogy lesson, I pointed out that Oholibamah appears both as a wife and as a clan name, so listeners should not confuse the two.
examples.analytical: Genesis 36 uses Oholibamah both as a personal name and as the designation of a clan chief, which shows how the text connects family and tribal identity in Edom.

nuance.analogy: Like a family name that became the name of a whole village: the person and the group share one name.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew name whose exact meaning is debated; often linked to 'tent of the high place', though uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing Oholibamah with Oholibah, the symbolic name in Ezekiel.
Using the RSV spelling 'Aholibamah' and the other spelling interchangeably without noticing they refer to the same name.
nuance.biblical_note: Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon the Hivite, is named as one of Esau's wives in Genesis 36:2 (RSV, spelled Aholibamah). Genesis 36:41 lists a clan chief called Oholibamah among the chiefs of Edom. Her marriage ties Esau's line to the local population of the land of Seir.

senses.definition: Tense, nervous; consequently irritable.
senses.example: Waiting to see who had been chosen, we were all on edge.

core.definition: Tense, nervous, and easily irritated, especially because of stress or uncertainty.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on EDGE, and 'on' is a weak, reduced vowel in fast speech. The final consonant is a voiced 'j' sound, so do not add an extra 'uh' after it.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes discomfort and irritability, though it is not severe.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say on edge about people who are anxious before a big event, a medical result, or a tense family situation. A natural response is 'Take a deep breath' or 'Try to relax'. It is common in casual talk and in friendly advice, but it can be too casual for formal reports, where anxious or tense is better.

distinctions.note: Nervous often refers to fear or worry about a specific event; on edge describes a more general tension that makes you irritable.
Anxious is more formal and clinical; on edge is everyday speech for feeling tense and easily annoyed.

examples.everyday: I've been on edge all day waiting for the doctor to call back about my test results.
examples.professional: The team has been on edge since the outage, so let's keep the stand-up short and focus on the fix.
examples.analytical: Public discourse in a crisis tends to keep citizens on edge, which can make rational deliberation harder to sustain.

nuance.analogy: Being on edge is like standing on a ladder with your weight shifting; you are alert and ready to jump at any small sound.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in edge' instead of 'on edge'.
Confusing the meaning with being at the edge of something; on edge describes a feeling, not a location.

conversation.text: I've been on edge all day waiting for the test results.
Everyone's on edge because of the rumors about layoffs.
The loud thunder had the dog on edge all night.
That horror movie had me on edge the whole time.

senses.definition: Excellent; bold; performing well.
senses.example: Her presentation was on point, and the board approved the budget in minutes.

senses.definition: Having a direct application to the case or topic under consideration; apposite, relevant.
senses.example: The judge's question was on point, cutting straight to the heart of the contract dispute.

senses.definition: On the tips of the toes; en pointe.
senses.example: The ballerina held her position on point for the final few bars of the music.

senses.definition: Having taken point; responsible for leading an operation; more generally, deployed and alert.
senses.example: The sentries stood on point at every gate while the convoy crossed the valley.

core.definition: Directly relevant to the matter being discussed, or executed exactly right; in informal speech, excellent.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on POINT, and 'on' is weak. Keep the oy diphthong clear, glide from aw to ee, and do not reduce the word to 'pent'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is a compliment for accuracy, relevance or style.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'on point' in work meetings to mean relevant, and in casual speech to mean excellent or spot-on, especially about style, food or performance. It is informal, so in formal writing use 'relevant' or 'pertinent' instead. A natural reply is 'Right? I thought so too.'

distinctions.note: Relevant is neutral and standard; on point adds a sense of precision and sharpness, often in a compliment.
Pertinent is formal and used mostly in writing or official settings; on point is more conversational.
Spot on means accurate or exactly right and is more common in British English; Americans more often say on point or right on.

collocations: the answer was right on point

examples.everyday: That burrito was on point, honestly. I'm coming back next week.
examples.professional: Your summary is on point, so let's send it to the client before the call.
examples.analytical: The critic's second objection is on point, since it targets the premise rather than the conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a dart landing exactly in the center of the bullseye.
nuance.etymology: From point, from Latin punctum, 'a prick'; the relevance sense comes from hitting the exact spot.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'on point' (relevant) with 'to the point' (direct and brief).
Using 'on point to' with a following preposition; the phrase is used alone or with 'with'.

on-point.etymology: Possibly from the French en pointe meaning to be on the tip of the toes in ballet and reflects a higher degree of skill.

senses.definition: Occurring once, independent of any pattern; one-time.
senses.example: The government insisted that the embarrassing loss of the tax records was a one-off event.

senses.definition: Special; remarkable; rare; unusual.
senses.example: Winning the national championship was a one-off, and nobody expected her to repeat it.

senses.definition: Something unique and remarkable.
senses.example: It is a one-off; there is nothing else like it.

core.definition: Happening or made once only, not part of a pattern or series; a single, unrepeated occurrence.

pronunciation.tip: Both parts get stress, with OFF slightly stronger, so say it as WUN-AWF with the 'aw' of 'caught'. Don't pronounce 'one' as 'oh-nee'; it is 'wun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a single event or item without judgment, though in some contexts it can suggest an exception that is unlikely to happen again.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'one-off' mostly in business, product, and project talk, such as 'a one-off payment' or 'a one-off event'. In everyday speech, 'one-time' is more common in American English ('a one-time fee'). If you mean something special and rare, say 'it's a one-of-a-kind' or 'it's a unique thing'.

distinctions.note: Nearly synonymous, but 'one-time' is the more standard American phrase for a single occurrence, while 'one-off' often implies an exception to a regular pattern.
A fluke is an unexpected stroke of luck or an accidental result, whereas a one-off is simply a single event that is not repeated.

examples.everyday: Don't worry about the late fee, it's a one-off, and I'll make sure it doesn't happen again.
examples.professional: The vendor billed us a one-off setup fee, so there are no recurring charges after onboarding.
examples.analytical: The election result looks like a one-off rather than evidence of a lasting political realignment.

nuance.analogy: Like a comet that crosses the sky once and never returns.
nuance.etymology: Compound of one and off; the root idea is a single item or event struck off from a series.
common_mistakes: Using 'one-off' for a regular or recurring event, which contradicts the meaning.
Writing 'one off' without a hyphen when it comes before a noun.

senses.definition: A chance for advancement, progress or profit.
senses.example: seize the opportunity

senses.definition: A favorable circumstance or occasion.
senses.example: Having a holiday is a great opportunity to relax.

core.definition: A chance to advance, make progress or gain something, or a favorable time or situation for doing something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TOO, the fourth syllable. Many Americans say 'tyoo' or 'too' for the middle, and the last syllable is a weak 'tee'. Don't say 'oh-PORT-unity'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a useful chance, though it can also be used to soften bad news.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word constantly in work and daily life: job openings, sales, promotions and invitations. Managers often say 'this is an opportunity to grow' to frame a hard situation positively. A polite reply to an offer or interview is 'Thanks for the opportunity'.

distinctions.note: Chance can mean luck or simple probability; opportunity is a favorable situation you can actually use to achieve something.
Possibility means something might happen; opportunity implies a useful chance you could act on.

examples.everyday: Thanks for inviting me to the barbecue, I'd love the opportunity to meet your neighbors.
examples.professional: This project is a real opportunity to show the leadership team what our forecasting model can do.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers treat each moral choice as an opportunity to become a different kind of person.

nuance.analogy: Like a door left open for a moment: it's there now, and it may close if you wait.
nuance.etymology: From Latin opportunitas 'fitness, convenience, favorable time', from opportunus 'fitting, timely'.
common_mistakes: Using 'opportunity' for any general chance; 'chance' often sounds more natural when no benefit is implied.
Using the wrong preposition: say 'an opportunity for growth' or 'an opportunity to grow', not 'opportunity of growth'.

opportunity.etymology: From *opportune* + *-ity*, from Middle French *opportunité*, from Latin *opportūnitās*.

senses.definition: (rare) A person who learns late in life.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A person who begins learning or studying something new late in life, often in older age.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AHP. The final -ath rhymes with 'math', with a short 'a' and a crisp 'th'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It praises late learning, but it is a rare, bookish term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use opsimath outside scholarly or literary writing. In everyday speech, people say someone who started learning late or who went back to school later in life. Calling someone an opsimath may sound learned or playful.

distinctions.note: Late bloomer is common and informal, describing someone who develops later in general; opsimath specifically refers to late learning.
An autodidact is self-taught at any age; an opsimath emphasizes learning that begins late in life.

examples.everyday: My grandmother started piano at seventy, so she is a true opsimath.
examples.professional: Our training program welcomes opsimaths, since mid-career engineers often bring valuable experience to data work.
examples.analytical: The essay treats the opsimath as a figure who challenges the assumption that intellectual growth belongs to youth.

nuance.analogy: An opsimath is like a late-blooming tree that flowers after others have already finished blooming.
nuance.etymology: From Greek opsimathēs, learning late, from opse, late, and manthanein, to learn.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, which is not the stressed syllable.
Using opsimath for a child who learns slowly; it refers specifically to late learning in adulthood.

opsimath.etymology: From the Ancient Greek *ὀψιμαθής* (“late in learning”), ultimately from *ὀψέ* (“late”) and *μανθάνω* (“I learn”); compare *opsimathy*, *philomath*, and *polymath*.

senses.definition: The fact of having a regular, proper and systematic arrangement.
Orderly behavior.
senses.example: The orderliness of the kitchen impressed the health inspector, who smiled as she left.

core.definition: The quality of being neat, systematic and well arranged, with everything in its proper place.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the r sound in 'or' and 'der.' The ending '-ness' is a reduced 'nus,' not 'nes,' and the middle 'li' is short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises careful organization and calm, systematic behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word more in writing, analysis or description than in casual talk. In everyday speech, people say 'neat,' 'organized' or 'tidy' instead. It is common in discussions of procedures, records, laboratories or public order, such as 'the orderliness of the evacuation.'

distinctions.note: Order can mean a general state or a command; orderliness refers specifically to the quality of being systematic and well arranged.
Tidiness concerns neat appearance, such as a clean desk, while orderliness concerns systematic arrangement and logical structure.

examples.everyday: I love the orderliness of my kitchen since I started using labeled bins.
examples.professional: The orderliness of our data pipeline made debugging much faster after the redesign.
examples.analytical: Hume questioned whether the orderliness of nature can be justified by reason alone.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-kept library where every book has its home.
nuance.etymology: Formed from orderly (order plus -ly) with the suffix -ness; order comes from Old French ordre, from Latin ordo.
common_mistakes: Using 'orderliness' for a single action; 'orderliness' names a quality, not an event.
Misplacing stress as or-der-LI-ness instead of AWR-der-lih-nus.

senses.definition: To arrange in working order.
To constitute in parts, each having a special function, act, office, or relation; to systematize.
senses.example: The committee organized the volunteers into teams, each responsible for one neighborhood.

senses.definition: To furnish with organs; to give an organic structure to; to endow with capacity for the functions of life.
senses.example: an organized being

senses.definition: To band together into a group or union that can bargain and act collectively; to unionize.
senses.example: the workers decided to organize; their next task was to organize the workers at the steel mill

senses.definition: To sing in parts.
senses.example: to organize an anthem

core.definition: To arrange things or people into a logical order or working system, or to plan and coordinate an event or effort.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on OR, and the middle syllable is a weak schwa, so say 'OR-guh-nyz,' not 'or-GAN-eyes.' Many learners add an extra syllable in the middle, so keep the word to two main beats.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. Organizing is generally seen as helpful and responsible, though it can sound controlling if someone organizes others without asking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use organize constantly for both physical tidying and planning events, such as 'organize the closet' or 'organize a fundraiser.' For a casual sense, you can say 'get things organized' or 'let's get organized.' Spelling in the US is always organize with a z, never organize.

distinctions.note: Arrange focuses on putting things in a particular position or pattern, while organize implies creating a system or sorting things into categories.
Coordinate emphasizes making different people or parts work together smoothly, while organize can also mean simply establishing a structure or plan.

examples.everyday: Can you help me organize the garage this weekend?
examples.professional: I'll organize the kickoff meeting and send everyone the agenda by Monday.
examples.analytical: Early civilizations organized labor around irrigation, which required central planning and record keeping.

nuance.analogy: To organize is like sorting a toolbox so every wrench and screwdriver has its own drawer, so you can find what you need quickly.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin organizare, from organum, 'instrument, tool,' which is also the source of organ.
common_mistakes: Using British spelling organise in American writing.
Saying 'organize about' or 'organize for' when you mean 'organize a meeting' or 'organize an event.'
Stressing the second syllable as 'or-GAN-ize' instead of OR-guh-nyz.

organize.etymology: From Middle English *organizen*, *organysen*, partly from Middle French *organiser* and partly from its etymon, Medieval Latin *organizō*, from Latin *organum* (“organ”).

senses.definition: The study of pronunciation.
Accepted or customary pronunciation.
senses.example: The speech coach drilled orthoepy, making sure every student said the vowels the way dictionaries recommend.

core.definition: The study of correct pronunciation, or the standard pronunciation of words in a language.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on THOH. The ending -epy is pronounced pee, and the middle vowels are reduced to a quick uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized term used by linguists, dictionary editors, and language teachers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use orthoepy in daily conversation. It appears in linguistics, dictionary writing, and discussions of standard pronunciation. In everyday speech, people say pronunciation or how to say a word.

distinctions.note: Orthography is the study of spelling, while orthoepy is the study of pronunciation.
Phonetics studies the physical sounds of speech in general, while orthoepy focuses on the accepted pronunciation of a language.

examples.professional: Our dictionary team updated the orthoepy notes for the new entries.
examples.analytical: Debates over orthoepy reveal how a community decides which pronunciation counts as standard.

nuance.analogy: Orthoepy is like a referee for speech, deciding which pronunciation is the accepted one.
nuance.etymology: From Greek orthoepeia, meaning correct speech, from orthos right and epos word.
common_mistakes: Confusing orthoepy with orthography, which concerns spelling.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first part of the word.

orthoepy.etymology: From Ancient Greek *ὀρθοέπεια*, possibly via Latin *orthoepia*, from Ancient Greek *ὀρθός* (“correct”) + *ἔπος* (“word”) + *-ία* (“-y”).

senses.definition: To transform (or cause to transform) from a softer animal substance into bone; particularly the processes of growth in humans and animals.
senses.example: Doctors watch the child's wrist X-rays to see how the bones ossify as he grows.

senses.definition: To become (or cause to become) inflexible and rigid in habits or opinions.
To grow (or cause to grow) formulaic and permanent.
senses.example: Over decades, the committee's rules ossified into rituals no one questioned anymore.

senses.definition: (rare) To calcify.
senses.example: With age, the old artery walls began to ossify, stiffening under the cardiologist's watch.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To harden into bone, or to become rigid and unchangeable in habits, opinions or structures.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a quick schwa, and the final syllable rhymes with 'my'.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ossify to describe rigid thinking, bureaucracy, or institutions that stop changing, usually with disapproval. For example, a company or policy that becomes unable to adapt has ossified. In medicine or biology it describes bones forming, but in everyday talk the figurative sense is much more common.

distinctions.note: Harden is a general word for becoming firm or unyielding, while ossify suggests becoming completely rigid over a long time.
Stagnate emphasizes lack of growth or movement, while ossify emphasizes becoming hard and fixed.

examples.everyday: My uncle's opinions about cars have ossified, and he won't listen to anything new.
examples.professional: If we keep the same review process for five years, it will ossify and nobody will want to change it.
examples.analytical: Religious movements often begin as living communities but ossify into rigid systems that resist reform.

nuance.analogy: Like a soft clay that dries and hardens into a fixed shape, ideas can ossify until they can no longer be reshaped.
nuance.etymology: From Latin os (bone) and -fy (to make), formed in English.
common_mistakes: Using it for simple hardening of objects; it usually describes a process of becoming rigid over time.
Mispronouncing the stress as oss-SIFF-eye.

ossify.etymology: or modeled on French *ossifier* and formed from Latin *os*, *ossis* (“bone”) *ify*.

senses.definition: The quality of being otherworldly.

core.definition: The quality of seeming to belong to a spiritual or fantastical realm rather than ordinary life; a detachment from everyday concerns.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'WURLD', with a light secondary stress on the first syllable. Keep the 'd' in 'world' and use a short 'ih' in '-li-' and a weak ending '-nuss', not a long 'ness'.

nuance.connotation: Can be positive, suggesting a calm, spiritual or artistic quality, or negative, suggesting someone is impractical or out of touch with reality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in book reviews, art criticism, and discussions of religion or personality, rather than in casual talk. Positive use describes a serene or mystical quality, while negative use describes someone who seems impractical. In everyday speech, people often say 'dreamy', 'spacey', or 'lost in its own world'.

distinctions.note: Spirituality is an active relationship with the sacred, while otherworldliness describes an impression or quality that seems to belong elsewhere.
Detachment means emotional or practical distance, while otherworldliness can also carry a mystical or artistic sense.
Unworldliness suggests naivete or inexperience, while otherworldliness suggests a spiritual or mysterious quality.

examples.everyday: There's a kind of otherworldliness in the way she plays the cello on the porch at dusk.
examples.professional: The brand wants the product to project otherworldliness, but customers still need clear battery instructions.
examples.analytical: Eliot's poetry blends otherworldliness with a sharp attention to the decay of ordinary urban life.

nuance.analogy: Like a song heard faintly through a wall, otherworldliness seems to come from a place just out of reach.
nuance.etymology: From otherworldly, from other, world and -ly, plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'worldliness', which means the opposite: involvement in everyday affairs and practical concerns.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'uh-thur-WUR-li-nuss', or dropping the 'd' in 'world'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the Greek word kosmos ('world') often means the human order that is opposed to God, rather than the created earth. Key passages are John 17:14-16 (the disciples are not of the world, as Jesus is not of the world, yet they are sent into it), John 18:36 (Jesus says his kingdom is not of this world) and Romans 12:2 (believers are told not to be conformed to this world but to be transformed).

senses.definition: Looking towards or thinking about other people, places, or things, rather than towards or about oneself.

core.definition: Focused on the wider world and other people, rather than on oneself or on one's own group or concerns.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the first word, OUT, with a lighter stress on LOOK. The word 'outward' is reduced to 'OUT-wurd', and the -ing ending is a short 'ing'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: suggests openness, generosity and interest in others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use outward-looking in policy, business and community contexts, such as 'an outward-looking company'. In casual talk they say 'open-minded' or 'really connected to the community'. It sounds formal in conversation but natural in writing.

distinctions.note: Open-minded describes willingness to consider new ideas, while outward-looking describes attention to the external world and other people.
Extroverted describes social energy in personality, while outward-looking describes where a person or group focuses attention.
Global describes scope or geography, while outward-looking describes an attitude toward the outside world.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is so outward-looking; she volunteers at the shelter and always asks about my family.
examples.professional: Our team needs to be more outward-looking, so we talk to customers before we build new features.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that a Christian ethic must be outward-looking, directed toward the neighbor rather than toward the believer's own moral progress.

nuance.analogy: Like a window rather than a mirror: you look out at the world instead of at your own reflection.
nuance.etymology: From outward (out plus -ward) and looking, the present participle of look.
common_mistakes: Writing 'outward looking' without the hyphen in formal writing, where the hyphen is expected.
Confusing outward-looking with outward, which can mean external appearance rather than attention to others.

senses.definition: An excess of what is needed or is appropriate.

core.definition: An excess of something; more of it than is needed, wanted, or appropriate.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on BUN, and the middle syllables are reduced to schwa sounds. The ending is -ance, pronounced -uhns, not -ants; many learners say 'uh-BUN-dints' by mistake.

nuance.connotation: Negative in most uses, because an excess is usually a problem, such as an overabundance of meetings or work. It can be neutral when describing supply, as in an overabundance of tomatoes in the garden.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'overabundance' for a surplus that causes problems or looks wasteful, such as an overabundance of options or caution. In casual conversation, people usually say 'way too much' or 'too many' instead. It sounds more polished in writing, presentations, and reports.

distinctions.note: 'Surplus' is a neutral economic or practical term for extra supply beyond what is needed, while 'overabundance' often implies a problem.
'Glut' suggests an oversupply that depresses prices or overwhelms a market, which is more specific than the general 'overabundance.'
'Excess' is a general word for too much, while 'overabundance' adds a sense of richness or plenty that goes beyond need.

examples.everyday: We have an overabundance of tomatoes from the garden this year, so come take some home.
examples.professional: The project suffers from an overabundance of dashboards and too few clear metrics.
examples.analytical: Thinkers from Plato onward have worried that an overabundance of choice can paralyze judgment rather than free it.

nuance.analogy: Like a grocery cart so full that nothing fits anymore: more is not always better.
nuance.etymology: From 'over-' and 'abundance,' from Latin abundantia, from abundare, 'to overflow.'
common_mistakes: Using 'overabundance' for something pleasant without a negative sense, which can sound odd.
Writing 'overabundence' with an -ence ending; the correct spelling is -ance.
Stressing the first syllable instead of BUN.

senses.definition: Because of, on account of.
senses.example: I gave up my job as a typist owing to repetitive strain injury.

core.definition: Because of; as a result of; caused by.

pronunciation.tip: Stress OH-ing, then reduce 'to' to a quick tuh in normal speech. Link the phrase so it sounds like OH-ing-tuh, with no pause.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is factual and somewhat formal, and it is often used in explanations or apologies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use owing to mainly in writing, news reports, announcements and formal explanations, such as 'the flight was delayed owing to weather.' In everyday speech most people say because of or because. It is a common and correct choice in workplace emails and reports.

distinctions.note: Because of is the everyday choice in both speech and writing; owing to sounds more formal and is common in reports.
Traditional usage says due to modifies a noun and owing to modifies a verb, but many Americans use them interchangeably, so either is acceptable in most contexts.

examples.everyday: Our flight got delayed owing to the storm over Chicago, so we will be late.
examples.professional: The launch slipped two weeks owing to a data pipeline bug we found late in testing.
examples.analytical: Owing to the limits of the sample, the study cannot be generalized beyond urban adults.

nuance.analogy: Like a row of dominoes, where one event tips the next.
nuance.etymology: Owing (from owe, 'be caused by') plus to, from Old English agan.
common_mistakes: Following owing to with a clause: say 'owing to the rain' or 'because it rained', not 'owing to it rained'.
Using owing to casually in speech where because of sounds more natural.

senses.definition: The alleviation of pain, typically by means of medication.

core.definition: The reduction of physical pain, usually through medicine, treatment, rest or therapy.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on relief, with a lighter stress on pain. Say the second word as rih-LEEF with a reduced first vowel, and in fast speech the words link smoothly as 'payn-ri-LEEF'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it is a helpful, comforting term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pain relief for medicine or treatment, as in 'Do you have anything for pain relief?' at a pharmacy. Asking for something for pain is more casual. A natural reply is 'Try ibuprofen, and take it easy for a day.'

distinctions.note: A painkiller is a specific medicine, while pain relief is the general result or process of feeling less pain.
Anesthetic is a clinical term for medicine that numbs or blocks sensation, often used during surgery.

examples.everyday: Do you have anything for pain relief? My knee is killing me.
examples.professional: The clinic offers pain relief options, including physical therapy and short-term medication, for patients after surgery.
examples.analytical: Debates about opioids often pit fast pain relief against long-term risk, which makes policy hard to settle.

nuance.analogy: Pain relief is like a dam that lowers the water level: it doesn't stop the rain, but it keeps the flood from reaching you.
nuance.etymology: Compound of pain and relief, from Old French relief, meaning a lifting up, from relever, to lift up again.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on pain (PAYN ri-leef) instead of on relief.
Using relief alone as a verb for pain, as in 'relief my pain'; say 'get pain relief' or 'relieve my pain'.

senses.definition: A substance that is applied as a liquid or paste, and dries into a solid coating that protects or adds color to an object or surface to which it has been applied.
senses.example: fresh coat of paint

senses.definition: A set of containers or blocks of paint of different colors/colors, used for painting pictures.
senses.example: Her grandmother gave her a wooden box of paints for her tenth birthday.

senses.definition: The free-throw lane, construed with the.
